name: Chain of Responsibility
intent: Pass a request along a chain of handlers until one of them deals with it.
scenario: Expense requests need approval. A manager approves up to $1,000, a director up to $10,000, and the CEO anything above. The request goes to the first one who can approve it.
problem: Which approver handles a request depends on the amount. A single function with if/else for every level knows all approvers and their limits. Adding a level, or skipping one on holiday, means editing that function.
solution: Give each approver the same interface and a reference to the next approver. Each one either handles the request or passes it on. The client sends the request to the first link and does not need to know who ends up handling it.
pain: One function knows every approver and every limit
Adding a level means editing that function
Skipping an approver is impossible without changing code
benefits: Each approver knows only its own limit and the next link
A new level is a new handler inserted in the chain
Chains can be built or reordered at runtime
The client sends to the first handler and is done
whenToUse: More than one object may handle a request and the handler is not known in advance
You want to decouple the sender from the receivers
Middleware pipelines, event bubbling, validation steps, approval workflows
whenNotToUse: There is exactly one known handler: call it directly
Every step must run (that is a pipeline, not a chain where the first match wins)
Guaranteed handling is essential and a silent fall-off the end would be dangerous
pitfalls: A request may reach the end of the chain unhandled
Long chains are hard to debug: who handled it?
Accidental cycles in the chain loop forever
Order matters and is easy to get subtly wrong

roles.label: Handler
roles.description: Interface/base class: handle a request or pass it to the next.

roles.label: Concrete Handler
roles.description: One link in the chain with its own rule.

roles.label: Client
roles.description: Sends the request to the first handler.
